records.title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
records.author: blimmer
records.storyText:
Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave.

PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again.

Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important.

PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically.

1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results.

2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355...

3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc.

4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely.

PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge.

Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate.

On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code.

We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits.

If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

records.title: Show HN: Rouler – Steer Windows traffic per app or IP across multiple interfaces
records.author: brndnbuilds
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

Rouler is "rules for your routes". It allows you to steer network traffic across multiple network interfaces on Windows. For example:

- Run Tailscale, Mullvad and OpenVPN official clients simultaneously.

- Use Rouler to send Slack via the OpenVPN connection, Chrome + an IP range via Tailscale and a torrent client via Mullvad.

Rouler is VPN agnostic, so you can "split-tunnel" with anything that sets up a windows network interface.

I'm an independent developer from Australia and have been working on Rouler for a bit over a year. It's been a challenging project to say the least, but I'm really happy with how it's turning out. I have spent a great deal of time building and throwing things away, starting over, belting the initial poc into something that I find intuitive... hopefully others do too!

I've done all the testing, fixing and improving I can, so now it's open for public beta. I'd love to hear your feedback... and there are some specific points I'm interested in hearing about listed on the Rouler website. Please reply with any questions you might have.

Thanks for reading!

Brendan

p.s. Rouler is "built in Rust" TM ;-)

---

On AI (skip if you're sick of hearing about it):

Since AI is the hot topic and people are naturally cautious about it, I'll add some quick notes about it, specifically about the driver development as that's the key thing to get right. The driver is hand written and every detail has been poured over many times over. I spent somewhere around 6-9 months manually building and testing just the driver, staring at Dbgview logs, wireshark logs, windows route tables, restarting VM's back to their snapshot and manually copying things across to start again. That's not always the most efficient way of doing things, but it's the way it had to be done. If I had tried to vibe code it Rouler simply wouldn't exist. I did try to lean on AI at times, but it constantly sent me in the wrong direction, told me things weren't possible, tried to take shortcuts and implement poor performing trade-offs. It also loved to hallucinate the windows api. Keep in mind this was around the Opus 4.1 - 4.6 days.

Outside of the driver, in user mode land, AI has crept more and more into my workflow. I've had a lot of success utilising the latest models in the app in particular, and I purposefully separated the UI and core logic so I'm able to quickly iterate on the UI. I've also found AI very useful for scripting and refactoring. It has built some great scripts that would've taken me days or weeks to build and fine tune.

records.title: Show HN: Jev in action – task classifier and auto model router in Keen Code
records.author: mochow13
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

In Keen Code, a coding agent solo-developed by me, I have implemented a task-classifier using Jev and a simple auto-router based on the classification result. The article shares details about how it's implemented.

In short, it has a very simple idea:

- For every user message, ask Jev to classify the task in one of the three categories (simple, standard, complex) given current state of the conversation.

- Keen also asks Jev to put a probability on this question: "is this a new task?"

- Based on the result, Keen uses a heuristic to switch the current model to one of the three pre-configured models by user for the three categories

- To make the router work, users have to configure one model per task category inside the coding agent itself

The heuristic is also very simple:

When routing is enabled, Keen switches only if the selected-category probability is greater than 0.5 and either:

- new-task probability is at least 0.6; or - category probability is greater than 0.8 and the target category is a higher tier than the active routed model.

Thoughts and feedback are welcome. And if you are interested to know more about Keen Code, the repo can be found here: https://github.com/mochow13/keen-code

records.title: Show HN: Proxium – Self-hosted HTTP/SOCKS5 proxy with a web admin UI
records.author: koldakov
records.storyText:
With the team we are building a network management tool: switch upgrades, data collection/analytics, etc. With the write operations on production switches we've been requested to add an AAA flow so we have only 1 entry point for all microservices. For that reason we decided to add a proxy in the first place, so each request goes through the proxy, authenticates with External Authentication (the first A), then proceeds to the next step etc.

First we thought about squid/envoy, but these proxies were declined by our devops as planned for the future. For sure we found a workaround, but then I thought why there are almost no proxies with UI/ACLs/limits/quotas/speed limits etc.

So I decided to create my own solution that works out of the box with 1 simple command:

  docker run -d --name proxium -p 80:80 -p 8080:8080 -v proxium:/var/lib/proxium \
    -e SUPERUSER_CREATE=true -e SUPERUSER_EMAIL=admin@example.com \
    -e SUPERUSER_PASSWORD=change-me ikoldakov/proxium
Then open http://localhost, log in, create a proxy account and use it: curl -x http://username:password@localhost:8080 https://ifconfig.me curl -x socks5h://username:password@localhost:8080 https://ifconfig.me

Also, proxium supports https for the admin panel with self-signed certificates, let's encrypt certificates or your own uploaded ones. The proxy itself supports TLS too (self-signed, uploaded or imported from certbot).

External auth is not supported yet, but it's next in the roadmap: an HTTP hook in nginx auth_request style first, then JWTs from your identity provider. SSO over OIDC for the admin panel is planned as well.

I used AI for some parts of the code

Hello HN!

My name is Sam and this is Craig. Craig is a local-first TUI for managing AI coding agents. It’s agent-agnostic, creates isolated worktrees by default, and has a rich CLI for the agent to interact with to manipulate state and perform actions in the TUI.

I started building Craig when I got a job offer at a shop that was using Cursor. I was previously using Claude Code with Conductor and really enjoyed this type of experience. However Conductor didn’t support Cursor at the time and I wasn’t a big fan of the Cursor 3 Agents interface. For personal projects I was using mostly Codex with some Claude Code. Switching between tooling was frustrating. Around the same time I also started really enjoying the agent CLIs and how they just “felt good”.

Craig kind of builds on that and I think of it as a heads-up display and controls around the CLI. With the TUI being keyboard-driven you can get into a nice multi-task flow and move around pretty quickly. The UX is made to be low friction and high signal-to-noise.

To get started you can run `npm install -g craig-cli`, launch your favorite terminal (I like Ghostty), pop it in fullscreen and run the `craig` command. Once you launch it you can create a workspace, this can be a single repo directory or multiple. Then create a new task under the workspace to launch Cursor, Codex, or Claude. Do your thang, and use your agent to create a PR. You’ll see Craig automatically sync that PR, poll for checks and let you know when the PR is ready to merge. Merge it and keep moving in the same thread or start a new one.

I’d love for you to give it a try and let me know what you think - any feedback is greatly appreciated.

records.title: Show HN: Dovepass – can I legally fly a drone along this exact path in SF?
records.author: nimitmehra
records.storyText:
Dovepass answers one question for drone operators: given two points, can a drone legally fly between the two points?

I build route planning for delivery drivers and wanted to check what it would look like if the vehicle flies. Drone navigation is different from land-based vehicle navigation. In addition to road and traffic data, it requires data on buildings, building height, wind speed and direction, and total load, including the payload a drone might carry. It is also governed by a set of rules; depending on the area, federal, state, or county rules may apply.

The decision point becomes whether, at each point on the route the drone can fly based upon whether regulations permit, the wind direction favours it and whether it flying over a road or people? Depending on when the drone flies, the same path valid two hours ago may no longer be valid.

For example a trip from 24th & Valencia ( Mission) to 19th Ave & Irving (Inner Sunset) and back is 5.1 km each way. A DJI mini 4 Pro would take 19 min on 7 mph winds from the west and use 92% of its usable battery and give a Go signal with warning. But at 11mph wind from the same direction would become No-Go because it would use 111% of its usable battery. Or whenever there is a Giants game at Oracle Park, this route is unusable because it is 2.5miles from the stadium. FAA bars all drones within 3 nautical miles from a stadium from 1 hour before the game to one hour after it ends.

I chose San Francisco as the first city to build this because there is enough data about the buildings (92% coverage), wind data is easily available at the drone flying height, and the city has a mix of slopes, water bodies, buildings and airport-related airspace restrictions all in one city. The city also has local rules regarding drone flights in parks - both operated by the city as well as by Golden Gate National recreational areas ( National Park Service).

I used kimi to build it and claude acted a sa judge. To understand more about the challenges faced during the build and the tradeoffs made please read - https://dovepass.com/how-it-was-built/"

records.title: Show HN: Flyingcar.pet – a physics simulation of Tesla's flying Roadster stunt
records.author: closetheloopdev
records.storyText:
Hi HN. I kept watching the Tesla Roadster's flying video and wondered how much force would be required to pull off a stunt like that since it seemed unreal to me, so I asked Claude Opus 5.5 to create a simulation for me.

I gave Opus one task: look at the video and create a simulation like that using three.js, matching the video as closely as possible. I'd thought that Opus would one- or two-shotted this since in my mind it was just estimating height and distances and working backwards to compute the thrusts. Little did I know this would turn into a multi-day project.

Opus's first hurdle was recognizing the five parked Tesla vehicles. The video was dark, so it was hard for Opus to see. I helped it identify the models and also gave it the approximate dimensions of all six Tesla vehicles, including the Roadster.

1. The initial version looked close enough to the video, but Opus made the car fly straight, whereas the video shows the Roadster veering to the left and landing to its left, so I asked Opus to watch the video again and correct that.

2. The next version showed the car drifting to the left mid-flight like the video, but the position was off when I compared frame by frame to the video. It turned out that Opus was being lazy and used only a few frames as reference instead of doing it frame by frame.

3. Once Opus matched the car position to the video, frame by frame, I realized that the roll did not match, so I asked Opus to investigate and redo.

4. The next version had the position and roll correct, but I did not see any thrusters firing during flight. It turned out that Opus was creating a smooth trajectory where the thrusters only fired for the launch and the landing, and stayed off mid-flight. This was not what I'd seen in the video, however.

5. Opus then changed it so that the thrusters would fire during the flight, which would affect the trajectory continuously. However, at this point I realized something odd: it was firing a thruster upward, which is in the opposite direction of the four bottom-mounted thrusters. It was definitely strange since the video did not show any upward-firing thrusters. It turned out that Opus was using 12 thrusters in total because it relied on Elon Musk's comment in 2018 that the Roadster would have around 10 thrusters. Using 12 thrusters was what allowed it to create any trajectory it wanted to. I asked it to use only 6 thrusters: four bottom ones for lifting and landing, and two side thrusters mounted near the front wheels since those were the ones I could see firing in the video.

6. Opus gave me another simulation with 6 thrusters firing, but now I could not see the side thrusters firing at all during the flight, which is similar to #4. It turned out that up to this point, Opus had been doing the simulation under the ideal conditions where the trajectory was pre-computed instead of doing a closed-loop control and constantly adjusting the thrust to keep the car on the planned path. Opus then added wind gusts and redid the simulation using a 100 Hz feedback loop.

At this point, I have something that is close enough to the video. It is still not perfect since I would love to match the firing sequence, intensity, and cloud shape of the thrusters during the flight, but I think this is a good stopping point for me, and now I have something where I can tweak the params like the car's weight, max thruster force, max height, number of rolls, etc. and model any flight path I'd like. There are a lot of params to configure, and some combinations can result in invalid flight paths, so I added WebMCP so that we can use the Claude plugin for Chrome to drive the simulation and ask the AI any questions. I found that Sonnet 5.5 Medium is good enough for this. Haiku 5.5 Medium is fast but also makes mistakes.

Caveats: the mass, drag coefficients, thruster positions and gas performance are estimates, not Tesla data. The closed-loop model also assumes perfect sensors.

records.title: Show HN: Stop Claude Code from compacting mid-task
records.author: LippInc
records.storyText:
I run long sessions with Claude. For a long time I've had Claude in the middle of some difficult coding task, and then I see the auto-compact message pop up. Every time I wonder if Claude actually picks everything up correctly and nothing is lost. Claude told me 78/82 auto-compactions landed while Claude was working. For a while I couldn't do much. At first I made a skill that would make Claude explicitly save progress throughout long runs. But that didn't fix the core problem and cost more tokens as well. Now that mods came out, I fixed the actual problem.

catnap tells Claude at 50% context what the context is and that it should finish what it's working on, write a handoff, and then initialize compaction itself. When Claude finishes its task, catnap compacts, and Claude can then pick up work again. The handoff replaces Claude Code's default summary, so we don't do similar work twice. If Claude for some reason doesn't compact before 60%, it gets a stricter note. And Claude Code's default auto-compact kicks in at 70% as a backstop. The 3 numbers are all settings.

After I took on catnap, 0 of 129 naps came mid-task: 98 of them in benchmarks and 31 in my own sessions.

The cost is the same as the default auto-compact kicking in at the same point, in tokens and dollars, on 200K and 1M context windows. Compared to the default auto-compaction that kicks in when context is nearly full, catnap used 56% fewer tokens. But lowering the default auto-compact will get you most of the way there as well.

I measured memory today as well. Claude worked through tasks one message at a time while 20 instructions and facts were said in the chat, inside long chatty messages, and nowhere else. Asked right after compaction to list them from memory, no file reads: all 20 were listed with catnap and with the default compaction, in every run (15 with catnap, 5 with the default). So in my tests the memory was exactly the same, but catnap got there with a handoff 60% shorter (4.0K tokens against 10K).

I was surprised that catnap is actually faster than the default option. This wasn't even one of the reasons I wanted to make this, it just happened. Since Claude writes the handoff in one go instead of the separate summary call the default makes, and the note is shorter, tasks finish sooner: measured end to end, 406 seconds instead of 464.

Try it with nothing installed:

  npx github:LippInc/catnap
It prints how often auto-compact cut in mid-task in your own logs (reads numbers only, sends nothing).

Install (needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or later, where mods are on by default):

  claude plugin marketplace add LippInc/catnap
  claude plugin install catnap@lippinc
Currently Claude Code only, tested on Windows and Linux. The memory test used made-up coding tasks on a 200K window.

Some related tools: compact-adviser, handoff-compact, session-pilot and sub-agent-compact. What catnap adds: Claude finishes its piece first, and the numbers on where the cut lands.

VM is a mail reader that runs inside GNU Emacs, a once popular mail client brought back to life as a community project. VM 9.0.0 is the first major release since the revival, with many bug fixes and new features.

VM features:

- Non-blocking IMAP and POP access, so you can fetch and save mail while carrying on in Emacs.

- IMAP and POP mailboxes cached on disk, so a folder stays accessible when the server is unreachable.

- Virtual folders: a folder view of messages across multiple folders, chosen by selection criteria.

- MIME support with inline and external display.

- HTML mail displays on a stock Emacs, through shr, the renderer eww uses.

- Folders in plain mbox format, and mboxcl2, which does not irreversibly quote lines starting with "From ".

- PGP access with EasyPG, Emacs's standard gpg interface.

- A configuration check, M-x vm-check-configuration to assist in setup.

- Emacs 28.1 or later.

- Extensive documentation.

- and much more

To install from NonGNU ELPA:

  M-x package-install RET vm RET
or via make from the source tree.

The NEWS-3.md file in the package lists everything in this release.

records.title: Show HN: Daisy – macOS software KVM with native trackpad gestures
records.author: tdewitt
records.storyText:
I have three laptops on my desk most days. Each laptop is used for different work, that I need to keep separate. (Day job, advisory work, personal.) When I went looking for a software KVM, the only free one that correctly handled trackpad gestures was Apple's Universal Control but that requires using the same iCloud account on each system, which is a non starter.

I had planned to just contribute to something else but the best option I found was intended to be a universal software KVM and had already rejected OS specific features. I get the thinking and don't begrudge the devs at all but I needed something that supports my workflow. Thus, Daisy (as in "daisy chain").

Daisy is a FOSS software KVM for macOS that doesn't need an iCloud account and handles gestures the way I want it to. You arrange the displays to match your physical desk, move the pointer across an edge, and control follows it to the next machine. Nothing leaves the local network (unless you want auto-updates) and there's encryption all the way around anyway.

It turns out that getting the trackpad working is somewhat non trivial. macOS doesn't expose Spaces and Mission Control swipes through the public gesture events. They arrive as private DockControl events, which meant figuring out how to capture the gesture phases, progress, and velocity, transport them, and replay them on another Mac. There's a fair amount of undocumented macOS behavior involved, and I've documented what I figured out in the repo.

Beyond gestures, the key things I wanted:

- Capable of handling a large chain (8), with a layout tool that that makes it easy to arranges systems the way they exist on my desk - Copy/paste across machines for images, files, and folders - No accounts or other external dependencies - Keeping displays active across the whole chain when you're doing work, without violating the intent behind screen locking - No single machine acting as the control system that all peers must negotiate with for trust (the machine you're typing on is always the control system)

It's not quite 1.0. Occasionally the layout UI loses track of a peer even though the connection is fine, input can sometimes get jerky, and I still need to beat on file transfers more.

I use it daily, though, and it's reached the point where I find it genuinely useful. It currently requires Apple silicon and macOS 26 or later. I've tested on 26 and 27.

Code, downloads, and the technical documentation are here: https://github.com/misfitdev/daisy

I'd be particularly interested in hearing from anyone who's fought with macOS input events or tried to solve the same problem. And if you give Daisy a shot, I'd like to know what breaks.

I'm also really happy about the security design and I'd love for people to poke holes in it. :)

records.title: Show HN: Search for AI-agents and usefulness score
records.author: Ayobamiu
records.storyText:
We presented this project at innovationintelligencehackathon.com and today we are putting a url out for you to test and give us feedback. after talking to teams building agents that research companies to create outreach, we found few things that are very important to them. one of them is recency. When we prompted agents with outdated alert about companies, 4 out of 7 times, they came up with outdated insights, even when they had recent news in context. A bigger model didnt fix it. So we built search for ai-agents with usefulness score on top. So, when you search each page comes with score+price.

this solve 3 problems;

1. token, SOTA agents read all pages to make sense of the useful ones

2. cost, when agents pay for pages they read, its is cost-effective to read only useful ones

3. quality, our score consider the task/query at hand and score useful pages, increasing quality of answers.

we want to find out fast if we are really up to something here. we'd love to hear from you.

records.title: Show HN: ULDA – Client-side encryption with a simple JavaScript API
records.author: nonsence
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Vitalii. Mark Shaposhnik and I have been building ULDA, a library intended to make client-side encryption easier to use in applications.

It started with our own project: we needed to authorize updates to client-side encrypted data without maintaining identity-based user accounts. Mark designed the authorization model and built an early implementation; I developed it into the current SDK and tooling.

The JavaScript SDK works with JSON resources and handles client-side encryption, authorization of resource updates, and synchronization. Payload encryption uses AES-256-GCM through Web Crypto, while ULDA provides its own SHA-256-based authorization model.

We built ULDA Room, a shared furniture planner, to make this tangible. Send an invitation link to someone on another device and arrange the room together. Changes synchronize between participants, with room content encrypted before it reaches the server. No signup is required, and anyone with the full invitation link can read and edit the room.

To try it on your own, click “Open second window” and move an item. The encryption inspector lets you compare readable client data with an encrypted record stored on the server. Demo resources expire after 24 hours.

The SDK is source-available under our Community Source license.

Demo: https://demo.ulda.io/ Documentation: https://docs.ulda.io/ SDK: https://github.com/ulda-io/ulda-auth

We’d appreciate feedback on the developer experience. After trying the demo or browsing the docs, what feels unclear about the concept or API? If you try integrating the SDK, we’d also like to hear where you get stuck.
